verdict_rationale: Both referees regard the proof as mathematically correct; the only criticisms concern misleading or hard-to-parse wording that does not affect the technical argument. Therefore there are no genuine mathematical errors to annotate.

secondary_issues.description: The phrase “the graph-pair $(x,y)$ is not isolated inside $\operatorname{graph}(\pi)$ by any existential formula over $Q$” is misleading: under a natural reading it would mean something different from the property actually proved. The subsequent argument makes the intended meaning clear, namely that any existential formula true of $(x,y)$ also holds of some pair outside the graph.

The discussion of “high $I$-sort equality classes,” the “vector shift,” and pairs of positive and negative $R$-literals is difficult to parse; in particular, Reviewer 2 notes that calling a pair of elements a positive or negative $R$-literal is imprecise. These are terminology and clarity issues rather than mathematical defects.

verdict_rationale: All three reviewers state that the construction and proof are mathematically correct; no genuine mathematical defect is identified in the referee reports. The criticisms concern attribution, readability, unnecessary generality, and stylistic or organizational choices rather than invalid arguments.

secondary_issues.description: Reviewers 1 and 2, and also Reviewer 3 to a lesser extent, note that the construction is close to techniques from Turetsky and later related work, and that a publishable version should cite and discuss this literature.
Several reviewers criticize the proof as overly pedantic, especially the explicit coding of finite sets and domain elements and the detailed proof of computability of the constructed relations.

The overview uses terminology before it is introduced and includes phrases such as “copy-computability argument” and “as required by Turing reducibility,” which reviewers found confusing or misleading, though not mathematically wrong.

The proof repeatedly emphasizes a generalization to quantifier-free infinitary matrices. Reviewer 2 notes that, in the finite language and with finitely many variables and parameters, this is not a genuinely stronger assertion in any substantive sense, although the statement proved is still correct.

Reviewers object to some stylistic choices, including the nonstandard phrase “preserved and reflected,” the use of “gadget,” and the splitting of closely related observations into several separate lemmas.

Reviewer 2 comments that the algorithmic description for computing automorphisms of arbitrary copies is awkwardly written and could more clearly be phrased as a search for a finite sequence; however, the reviewer does not identify a mathematical error in the algorithm.

verdict_rationale: Both referees judge the construction and verification to be mathematically correct; no genuine mathematical defects were identified. The only issues raised concern attribution to related work and minor stylistic/expository choices.

secondary_issues.description: Reviewer 1 states that the construction is highly reminiscent of Turetsky’s technique and of related uses in work of Alvir, Greenberg, Harrison-Trainor, and Turetsky, and would require citation and discussion of this similarity. Reviewer 2 similarly recommends citing related work such as Turetsky, Csima--Rossegger, and Alvir--Greenberg--Harrison-Trainor--Turetsky.

Reviewer 2 notes that the structure is built in an infinite computable language, unlike some finite-language solutions; this simplifies the construction and is stylistic rather than a mathematical error.

The referees note minor presentational inefficiencies, especially in the proof that automorphisms of arbitrary copies are relatively computable, where some hard-coding and search details could be simplified. They explicitly state that these details contain no inaccuracies.

verdict_rationale: The proof’s central application of the Ash--Knight--Manasse--Slaman--Chisholm theorem is mathematically invalid. The stated theorem omits the required uniformity hypothesis for parameter-free $\Sigma_1$ definability, and the argument only establishes nonuniform computability of the transported graph of the automorphism. This invalidates the contradiction and the claimed negative answer.

errors.title: Misstated Ash--Knight--Manasse--Slaman--Chisholm theorem omits uniformity
errors.block_location: Step 6: Application of the Ash--Knight--Manasse--Slaman and Chisholm Theorem
errors.error_description: The quoted theorem is false as stated. The parameter-free version of the Ash--Knight--Manasse--Slaman--Chisholm theorem requires that the copies $f(R)$ be computable uniformly relative to $N\oplus C$, i.e. by a single fixed procedure working for all copies, not merely that each $f(R)$ be computable relative to its own oracle in a nonuniform way. Without this uniformity one only obtains a different, parameter-allowing/nonuniform form of definability, and the claimed parameter-free $L_{\omega_1\omega}$ $\Sigma_1$ definition does not follow. Since the proof’s contradiction depends entirely on this theorem producing such a definition, the argument collapses.

errors.title: Verification establishes only nonuniform computability, not the uniform hypothesis needed for definability without parameters
errors.errored_block: By the definition of $C$, every automorphism of $\mathcal{B}$ is computable relative to $\mathcal{B} \oplus C$. Therefore, $f \circ \pi \circ f^{-1}$ is computable relative to $\mathcal{B} \oplus C$. Because the atomic diagram of $N$ (viewed as a real in $2^\omega$) consists of the atomic diagram of $\mathcal{B}$ and the evaluations of the finitely many constants, the oracle $\mathcal{B} \oplus C$ is Turing equivalent to $N \oplus C$. Thus, $f(R)$ is computable relative to $N \oplus C$. This verifies the fourth hypothesis.
errors.block_location: Step 6, item 4 in the verification of the theorem’s hypotheses
errors.error_description: This passage proves only that for each copy $N$ and isomorphism $f$, the relation $f(R)$ is computable from $N\oplus C$ by some computation that may depend on the particular automorphism/copy. The correct theorem needed later requires a uniform computation of all such $f(R)$ from $N\oplus C$ by one fixed program. The assumption that the structure is computably $\mathrm{AUT}$-countable on a cone gives nonuniform relative computability of each automorphism, not such a uniform index. Hence the actual hypothesis needed to infer parameter-free $\Sigma_1$ definability is not verified.

secondary_issues.description: Reviewer 2 notes that the extra constants $\bar d=\pi(\bar c)$ are largely unused in the rigidity argument; this is not itself a mathematical error, since they are later included to match the parameters appearing in the question.

Reviewer 2 notes that invariance under automorphisms is presented as a hypothesis of the cited theorem even though it is not part of the usual formulation; the substantive mathematical failure is the missing uniformity requirement.

verdict_rationale: Both referees explicitly judge the proof mathematically correct. The reported problems are attribution/citation failures and presentation issues, not defects in the mathematical argument, so there are no mathematical errors to record.

secondary_issues.description: The lower-bound portion closely adapts Schwartz's work on optimal paper/Möbius bands without citation. Reviewers specifically note the terminology of bends/T-patterns, the T-pair lemma, the main geometric argument, and the notation/labels such as T, B, D, H, and t as requiring attribution.
The proof of the polygonal T-pair lemma is considered too terse: the functions used in the Borsuk--Ulam argument are not geometrically motivated, even though the argument is judged to work.

The six-triangle model proof would benefit from a diagram of the domain and range, and the switch from the E,C notation in the lemma statement to A,B notation in the proof is potentially confusing without a connecting explanation.
The notation for vertex links, using expressions such as B_i-A_{i+2}-B_{i+1}, is cryptic because the minus signs denote edges in a path graph rather than subtraction or a formal sum.
One reviewer notes that the final optimization/endgame in the lower-bound proof is somewhat inefficient, although it is mathematically valid.

verdict_rationale: The referees largely agree that the proof is mathematically correct. The only substantive concerns raised are attribution and clarity issues, especially in the PL approximation/embeddedness discussion; no referee identifies a false mathematical claim or an unsalvageable logical gap.

secondary_issues.description: The proof should explicitly cite Schwartz's work on optimal Möbius bands. Multiple referees note that the lower-bound strategy, especially the oriented-line/topological lemma and the final geometric optimization using the notation T, B, D, H, closely follows Schwartz's argument and should not be presented without attribution.

The embeddedness justification in the PL approximation lemma needs clarification: the notation \(\widehat E\) is introduced without definition, and the claimed \(C^1\) convergence of the maps \(\Psi=\widehat E^{-1}\circ\pi\circ F_0\) should be stated more precisely, since the approximating maps are piecewise linear/piecewise smooth rather than globally \(C^1\). Reviewers treated this as a clarification issue rather than a mathematical failure.

Several arguments are correct but unnecessarily opaque or lengthy: the cevian-lengthening proof could be simplified, the function \(b\) in the oriented-line lemma could be defined more geometrically, the term “leaf graph” is nonstandard, and the lower-bound geometry would benefit from a diagram.

There are minor local clarity issues, such as the undefined symbol \(\gamma\) in the boundary-shortening inequality and overly detailed quantitative calculations in the Sadowsky--Wunderlich input and scaling argument.

verdict_rationale: Both referees regard the proof as essentially correct and publishable after minor revisions. The genuine mathematical issues they identify are limited to a false edge-case statement in the canonical ruling lemma and an insufficiently precise justification of embeddedness for the PL secant approximation. The remaining comments concern citation, attribution, or exposition rather than mathematical validity.

errors.title: Canonical ruling lemma falsely asserts uniqueness of the containing triangle
errors.errored_block: \item Each \(L_t\) is contained in a single clean triangle and joins the two boundary components in the universal cover.
errors.error_description: The statement says that each leaf is contained in a single clean triangle, which is false if read as uniqueness: leaves corresponding to nonboundary edges of the triangulation are shared by two adjacent clean triangles, so they are contained in both. This is a genuine edge-case error in the formulation of the lemma, although it does not affect the later use of the lemma, since the proof only needs each leaf to be contained in at least one clean triangle and to be a straight clean segment that is lengthened.

errors.title: Embeddedness of the PL approximation is not justified as written
errors.errored_block:
For sufficiently small mesh, \(\bar f\) is an embedding.  Indeed, in bend coordinates the smooth map \(F\) has the form
\[
F(s,r)=(1-r)a(s)+r b(s),
\]
with \(a,b\) \(C^1\) boundary curves.  The above piecewise-affine maps are the usual secant approximations to this ruled embedding; they converge to \(F\) in \(C^1\).  A \(C^1\)-small perturbation of a compact \(C^1\)-embedded surface is again embedded.
errors.error_description: The proof asserts that the piecewise-affine secant approximations converge to the ruled embedding in \(C^1\) and then invokes stability of compact \(C^1\)-embedded surfaces under \(C^1\)-small perturbations. As written this is not a valid justification, because the PL approximations are only piecewise \(C^1\), not globally \(C^1\), so the claimed \(C^1\)-convergence and the subsequent perturbation argument require clarification or replacement by a direct embeddedness argument. The intended embeddedness statement is likely true, but this step leaves a gap in the proof of realizability.

secondary_issues.description: The lower-bound argument, especially the T-pattern and geometric squeezed-pattern lemmas, closely follows Schwartz's work and should cite it explicitly in that part of the proof rather than only in the later discussion of existence.

The discussion of the smooth existence theorem is inaccurately attributed: Sadowsky's construction is piecewise smooth and globally \(C^1\), while the globally smooth isometric embedding result should be attributed to Halpern--Weaver; the cited literature should be corrected.
The proof of the realization proposition would benefit from a brief explanation of the strategy and the roles of the auxiliary parameters \(w\) and \(\lambda\).

The geometric lower-bound argument could be made clearer with a figure or more conceptual explanation, and the diagonal-stretching argument in the PL approximation could be elaborated, though the referees did not identify these as mathematical failures.

verdict_rationale: The proof is not a complete solution. Its lower bound depends on applying a version of Schwartz's theorem whose hypotheses are not met by the affine squeeze-map surfaces in the problem, and its upper bound is only a heuristic construction with no rigorous verification of the required triangulation, squeeze inequalities, or embedding condition. It also contains an incorrect description of the limiting Möbius-band configuration used to motivate the construction.

errors.title: Unjustified application of Schwartz's theorem to non-isometric squeeze-map surfaces
errors.errored_block:
By Schwartz's Theorem on the optimal paper Moebius band (2023), any embedded ruled Moebius band in $\mathbb{R}^3$ with minimal ruling length $w$ and boundary length $L$ must satisfy $L \ge 2\sqrt{3} w$. 
Applying this to our polyhedral Moebius band $f(M)$, where all rulings are strictly greater than $1$, we obtain:
\[
2\beta > L \ge 2\sqrt{3}(1) = 2\sqrt{3} \implies \beta > \sqrt{3}.
\]
errors.block_location: Step 1: The Lower Bound, final paragraph
errors.error_description: The proof claims that Schwartz's theorem applies directly to the polyhedral Möbius band obtained from the map $f$. As the referees point out, Schwartz's theorem concerns paper Möbius bands satisfying piecewise smooth or piecewise isometric/developable hypotheses, whereas here $f$ is only assumed to be affine on clean triangles and to be a squeeze map: it contracts boundary edges and stretches the other two edges, so it is not an isometric embedding of the flat domain. Thus the stated theorem is either misstated as applying to arbitrary embedded ruled Möbius bands, or at least is being applied outside its hypotheses. Without proving an extension of Schwartz's inequality to these non-isometric affine squeeze surfaces, the lower bound $\beta>\sqrt3$ is not established.

errors.title: Incorrect description of the limiting optimal configuration
errors.errored_block: The absolute theoretical limit of the optimal paper Moebius band is a sequence of $6$ equilateral triangles folded flat into a single doubly-covered equilateral triangle of side length $2/\sqrt{3}$. This limit configuration has altitude $1$ (ruling length $1$) and perimeter $3 \times (2/\sqrt{3}) = 2\sqrt{3}$. However, being flat, it self-intersects.
errors.block_location: Step 2: The Infimum is $\sqrt{3}$, limiting-shape paragraph
errors.error_description: The proof says that the relevant limiting Möbius-band configuration consists of six equilateral triangles. The referees state that in Sadowsky's nearly optimal construction the limiting configuration consists of three equilateral triangles, not six. Although the numerical altitude and perimeter quoted are the expected limiting values, the geometric description and the computation leading to them are wrong or at least incoherent, so this paragraph cannot serve as a reliable basis for the subsequent realization construction.

errors.title: Upper-bound construction is only heuristic and does not verify the realization conditions
errors.errored_block: For any $\beta > \sqrt{3}$, the domain boundary length $2\beta$ strictly exceeds $2\sqrt{3}$. This slack allows us to ``open up'' the flat equilateral triangle into an embedded, non-self-intersecting Moebius band in $\mathbb{R}^3$ (resembling a highly folded twisted ribbon). By taking a sufficiently fine locally finite $G_{\beta}$-invariant clean triangulation of $\Sigma$, and scaling the embedding slightly such that the boundary strictly contracts to a length just below $2\beta$ while the internal thickness pushes out to ensure all cross-edges strictly exceed their domain lengths, we can satisfy all conditions of the affine squeeze map.
errors.block_location: Step 2: The Infimum is $\sqrt{3}$, proposed construction paragraph
errors.error_description: This paragraph asserts the existence of realizations for every $\beta>\sqrt3$ but gives only informal geometric language such as “open up” and “scaling the embedding slightly.” It does not define an explicit embedded Möbius band, construct a locally finite $G_\beta$-invariant clean triangulation of $\Sigma$, prove that the induced affine map on every triangle decreases the boundary edge and increases the other two edges, or verify the global identification condition $f(p)=f(q)$ exactly along $G_\beta$-orbits. These are nontrivial requirements in the problem statement, so the realization half of the theorem is left unproved.

secondary_issues.description: Reviewer 2 notes that the phrase “let the map $f$ have directional vectors $\vec X$ and $\vec Y$” is nonstandard and unclear; the intended meaning should be made explicit. This is primarily a wording issue, since the referees did not identify the surrounding cevian-length argument itself as a mathematical error.

verdict_rationale: The referees do not identify any genuine mathematical error in the arguments. They regard the proofs as sound and the unresolved small-p assertion as explicitly acknowledged rather than falsely proved. The issues raised are about citation, contextualization, and local exposition.

secondary_issues.description: The coloring criterion should be connected to the Manickam--Miklós--Singhi conjecture via the change of variables y_i=x_i-1/b, with appropriate citations and explanation. Reviewers also note that known results of Pokrovskiy imply the criterion in the range b\ge 10^{46}a, and hence give additional good p-values after using multiplicative closure.

The submission should better acknowledge prior related work, including the connection to the idea of Alon, Emek, Feldman, and Tennenholtz mentioned by a reviewer, and should expand the brief reference to Manickam--Miklos--Singhi type counts.

In the induction proof of the subcritical shifted unit-gap inequality, the notation S=R+c\zeta should be clarified: \zeta is one of the Bernoulli variables \zeta_i and c is the corresponding coefficient b_i.

Reviewers note minor organizational and presentation issues: the paper jumps between results, lacks some flow because it is a collection of partial progress, and would benefit from clearer equation referencing and contextual transitions.

verdict_rationale: The elementary positive cases at p=1/2 and p=1 and the counterexamples outside the claimed set are not challenged, but the proof of the interval 0<=p<=1/3 rests on two crucial auxiliary inputs. The first comparison inequality attributed to Hoeffding is false in the form used, and the second binomial mean-tail estimate is merely asserted from citations that do not state it in the required form. Thus the positive interval is not proved, so the classification proof is incomplete.

errors.title: False Hoeffding open-tail comparison used for the reduction to equal weights
errors.errored_block:
Hoeffding's theorem gives, for every real \(u\),
\[
\Pr\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_iX_i>u\right]
\ge
\inf_{N\ge1}
\Pr\!\left[\frac{X_1+\cdots+X_N}{N}>u\right].
\]
errors.error_description: The proof asserts that Hoeffding's theorem gives this one-sided open-tail comparison for arbitrary i.i.d. real-valued random variables and arbitrary convex weights. The referees point out that this statement is not contained in Hoeffding's paper and is false as stated: for example, if X takes values 0, 1, 2 with probabilities 0.1, 0.1, 0.8, respectively, then with weights 0.1,0.1,0.8 and threshold u=0.8 the left-hand probability is 0.899 while the corresponding equal-weight infimum is 0.9. Hence the displayed inequality cannot be used to prove Lemma \ref{lem:hoeffding}. Since Proposition \ref{prop:smallp} relies on this lemma to reduce arbitrary Bernoulli convex combinations to binomial averages, the proof of the positive interval is left without a valid reduction.

errors.title: Unproved binomial mean-tail estimate for all 0<p<=1/3
errors.errored_block:
For \(0<p\le1/3\), the first assertion is the classical binomial mean-tail estimate of Samuels and Jogdeo--Samuels; see \cite{Samuels1965,JogdeoSamuels1968}. In the form needed here, that estimate states exactly that for every \(N\ge1\),
\[
\Pr[X_{N,p}\ge \lceil Np\rceil]\ge p.
\]
errors.error_description: The proof treats the inequality Pr[Bin(N,p) >= ceil(Np)] >= p for every N and every 0<p<=1/3 as a quoted classical theorem, but the referees state that the cited Samuels and Jogdeo--Samuels papers do not contain this assertion in the required generality; for instance, one cited result is restricted to cases such as Np being an integer, and no derivation for arbitrary N and p is supplied. Thus the first part of Lemma \ref{lem:binomial} is not proved. Because Proposition \ref{prop:smallp} uses exactly this lower bound to show that the equal-weight binomial tails are at least p, the argument for \mathcal P(p) on [0,1/3] is incomplete.

secondary_issues.description: The reviewers also considered the approach to have low novelty, since the main argument is essentially a reduction to auxiliary inequalities plus elementary counterexamples.

verdict_rationale: The counterexamples and the elementary endpoint/symmetry arguments are not challenged by the referees, but the proof of sufficiency for the whole interval \(0<p\le 1/3\) rests on two external lemmas that are neither proved nor correctly sourced. Since these lemmas are essential to the reduction, the submitted proof does not establish the claimed classification.

errors.title: Unproved Hoeffding--Pinelis comparison lemma
errors.errored_block:
\begin{lemma}[Hoeffding--Pinelis comparison for weighted Bernoulli sums]
\label{lem:hoeffding}
Let \(0<\theta<1\), let \(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_m\) be i.i.d. Bernoulli\((\theta)\), and let
\(a_i\ge0\), \(\sum_i a_i=1\). Then for every real \(x\),
\[
\mathbb P\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^m a_i\xi_i<x\right)
\le
\sup_{n\ge1}
\mathbb P\!\left(\frac1n B_{n,\theta}<x\right),
\]
where \(B_{n,\theta}\sim \Bin(n,\theta)\).
\end{lemma}
errors.error_description: The proof states a comparison inequality asserting that every weighted Bernoulli left tail is bounded by the supremum of equal-weight binomial-average left tails, and then uses it as an external theorem. The referees report that the cited Hoeffding and Pinelis results do not imply this statement; in particular, the referenced Pinelis corollary does not exist, and Reviewer 2 notes that a closely related formulation appears to be an open conjecture. Thus the lemma is not established within the submission or by the cited literature. Since this lemma is the first step in the proof of sufficiency for \(0<p\le 1/3\), that part of the theorem is left unjustified.

errors.title: Unproved binomial tail inequality outside the cited special case
errors.errored_block:
\begin{lemma}[Ramanujan--Jogdeo--Samuels binomial inequality]
\label{lem:binomial}
If \(0\le \theta\le 1/3\) and \(B_{n,\theta}\sim \Bin(n,\theta)\), then
\[
\mathbb P(B_{n,\theta}<n\theta)\le 1-\theta
\]
for every integer \(n\ge1\).
\end{lemma}
errors.error_description: The proof invokes a binomial-tail inequality for all integers \(n\) and all \(0\le\theta\le 1/3\), but gives no proof. The referees state that the cited Jogdeo--Samuels paper does not contain the lemma as stated; Reviewer 2 specifies that it proves a stronger statement only in the special case where \(n\theta\) is an integer, and that deriving the submitted version would require additional monotonicity work that is not supplied. Therefore this key inequality is an unproved assumption. Since it is used to bound every term in the supremum in the \(0<p\le1/3\) sufficiency argument, the submitted proof of that interval is incomplete.

secondary_issues.description: The references are misrepresented: Hoeffding's cited theorem and the Pinelis paper do not provide Lemma 1 as stated, and the cited Pinelis Corollary 3.7 reportedly does not exist.
The citation to Jogdeo--Samuels does not directly support Lemma 2 as stated; at most it covers a special case or would require an additional derivation not included.

verdict_rationale: The coupling argument correctly establishes the inequality for p=0 and p=1/k, but the submission does not prove—and according to the referees falsely asserts—the necessity direction. It claims that all non-reciprocal p fail, while the referees note that more values of p satisfy the inequality universally. Thus the advertised characterization is incorrect/incomplete.

errors.title: False and unproved exclusion of all non-reciprocal values of p
errors.block_location: End of the proof, after the sufficiency argument
errors.error_description: The proof asserts that every value of p outside \(\{0\}\cup\{1/k:k\in\mathbb Z^+\}\) fails the desired universal inequality, but it supplies no construction of weights giving counterexamples; indeed the text explicitly admits this structural gap. More seriously, Reviewer 1 states that there are additional values of p for which the inequality does hold universally, and Reviewer 2 says the submission arrives at an incorrect conjecture for the answer. Therefore the necessity direction of the stated “if and only if” theorem is not merely unproved but false as stated, so the proof does not solve the problem.

secondary_issues.description: The coupling proof for the reciprocal cases is reported by both reviewers to be essentially the known argument of Alon, Emek, Feldman, and Tennenholtz, but the submission does not cite that source.

verdict_rationale: The submission proves a correct special case and a weaker hard-case bound, but it does not prove the stated dichotomy. The hard case is reduced to an averaged tightening estimate (EAT) which is explicitly left unproved and whose truth is not justified; thus the proof is only conditional.

errors.title: Unproved averaged tightening estimate leaves the hard case conditional
errors.errored_block:
The following estimate is sufficient for the desired theorem.  Take measurable
near-minimizers \(C_y^0\) with
\(\Mass C_y^0\le2\EFill_f(y)\); standard measurable selection in the
separable flat topology, or equivalently outer integration with
\(\varepsilon\)-minimizers, is enough for this formal step.  One needs
\begin{equation}\tag{EAT}\label{EAT}
 A_\Omega
 \le C\left(R_1I+\frac{I^2}{S_1q}\right)
 +\frac{C}{q}\int_Q\int_\Omega
       \Mass(C_y^0\llcorner{\mathcal B}_z)\,dy\,dz .
\end{equation}
errors.block_location: Section “A sufficient averaged hard-case estimate”, statement of (EAT)
errors.error_description: The proof of the desired second alternative depends on the displayed averaged tightening estimate (EAT), but no proof or established theorem is supplied for this estimate; the text only states that it is “sufficient” and that “one needs” it. Reviewers note that the argument merely reduces the original problem to (EAT), and it is not clear that (EAT) is true. Consequently, the hard high-aspect case remains unproved, so the submission is a conditional reduction rather than a proof of the problem’s dichotomy.

secondary_issues.description: In the proof of the central target plane lemma, the sentence explaining why the relative boundary terms vanish is potentially confusing: it depends on interpreting an “x_i-face” as a face where x_i is constant. Reviewer 1 regarded this as a small error or bad wording that is easily fixed, not a substantive defect in the argument.

Reviewer 3 found the word “Optimizing” for the combination of inequalities in the partial hard-case bound misleading; the step is mathematically correct but could be described more explicitly as multiplying powers of the two inequalities and taking a fifth root.

Several later notions and phrases, such as “source-local,” “exact-plaque bad set,” “quotient cochain,” “absorption algebra,” and “nonsaturated exact-plaque localization,” are not explained clearly enough, and the role of the exact-plaque Fubini estimate is not well motivated. These are presentation issues apart from the main missing estimate.

verdict_rationale: The referees agree that the proof is largely correct as a proof of its own conditional reduction, but it does not solve the original problem. It inserts a substantial additional estimate that is not among the original hypotheses and is not proved, and it only reaches a conditional version of one of the required alternatives.

errors.title: Main lower bound is assumed as an extra hypothesis
errors.errored_block:
Assume now that
\[
\int_{F^{-1}(B_0)}\sigma_1^2\,d\mu
\ge
c_d\sqrt{\frac{S_3}{S_2}}\,
\mu(F^{-1}(B_0)).
\]
Then
\[
\int_{B_0}\operatorname{Area}(z_y)\,dy
\ge
c_d\sqrt{\frac{S_3}{S_2}}\,
\mu(F^{-1}(B_0))
\ge
\frac{c_d}{9}
S_1S_2S_3S_4
\sqrt{\frac{S_3}{S_2}}.
\]
errors.block_location: Proof, final reduction beginning with “Assume now that”
errors.error_description: The proof derives the desired volume lower bound only after assuming the estimate \(\int_{F^{-1}(B_0)}\sigma_1^2\,d\mu \ge c_d\sqrt{S_3/S_2}\,\mu(F^{-1}(B_0))\). This estimate is not a hypothesis of the original problem and is not proved in the submission; the referees note that establishing such an estimate appears to contain essentially the main difficulty. Consequently the argument proves only a conditional statement, not the theorem requested in the problem.

errors.title: Only one conditional alternative of the original dichotomy is addressed
errors.errored_block:
we obtain
\[
R_1R_2R_3R_4
=
\operatorname{Vol}(R)
\ge
\frac{c_d}{9}
S_1S_2^{1/2}S_3^{3/2}S_4.
\]
errors.error_description: The final conclusion is only the second type of lower bound, and even that is obtained only under the extra unproved estimate above. As Reviewer 2 points out, the original problem involved a dichotomy including the alternative \(R_3R_4 \gtrsim S_3S_4\); the proof never treats the complementary situation or proves that this alternative holds when the assumed estimate is unavailable. Thus the submission does not establish the full statement of the original problem.

secondary_issues.description: Several reviewers found the theorem statement unusually long and difficult to parse, with many intermediate claims placed in the statement rather than in the proof.

The filling-volume estimates are proved at length but then not used in the subsequent argument; reviewers noted that this makes the organization misleading and obscures the missing step needed for the original problem.

A reviewer objected to the phrase that \(dx_1\wedge dx_2\) “vanishes” on the \(x_1\)- and \(x_2\)-faces. The intended statement is that its pullback to those faces vanishes; this is at most a wording issue rather than a substantive mathematical defect.

verdict_rationale: The proof’s only substantive input is a quoted “Guth” product estimate which the referees state is not a special case of the cited Proposition 9.1 and essentially restates the desired conclusion. Since the subsequent argument merely applies this unsupported theorem, the proof is mathematically incomplete.

errors.title: Unsupported quoted theorem falsely claimed to follow from Guth
errors.errored_block:
We shall use the following special case of Guth's product-domain estimate.
It is the case \(n=4\), \(k=2\), \(\dim X=1\), and \(\dim Y=2\) of
Proposition 9.1 in Guth's paper \cite[Proposition 9.1]{GuthAreaExpanding}.
The proof in \cite{GuthAreaExpanding} is obtained from the isoperimetric
profile of rectangles, the Almgren--Gromov complex-of-cycles formalism,
and the tightening argument developed in Sections 1, 3, 4, and 6 of that
paper; a fuller account appears in Guth's thesis \cite{GuthThesis}.

\begin{quotedtheorem}[Guth, specialized product estimate]\label{qt:guth}
There are constants \(\varepsilon_0>0\) and \(c_0>0\) with the following
property.

Let
\[
X=[0,a],\qquad I=[0,b],\qquad Y=[0,u]\times[0,v],
\]
with the product Euclidean metric, and let \(S\subset \R^4\) be a rectangle
with side lengths
\[
S_1\leq S_2\leq S_3\leq S_4.
\]
Suppose
\[
F:(X\times I\times Y,\partial(X\times I\times Y))\longrightarrow
(S,\partial S)
\]
is piecewise smooth, has non-zero degree, and satisfies
\[
\Dil_2(F)\leq 1.
\]
If
\[
a\leq \varepsilon_0 S_1
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
uv\leq \varepsilon_0 S_3S_4,

then
\[
\Vol_4(X\times I\times Y)
=abuv
\geq
c_0\,S_1S_2^{1/2}S_3^{3/2}S_4.
\]
\end{quotedtheorem}
errors.error_description: The proof asserts that the displayed product estimate is a special case of Proposition 9.1 in Guth’s paper, but the referees state that Proposition 9.1 does not give this theorem or anything resembling this conclusion. The quoted estimate is essentially the desired problem statement reformulated for the product decomposition of the domain. Because no valid proof or valid literature result is supplied for this estimate, the central theorem used in the argument is unsupported, so the subsequent deduction has no mathematical foundation.

errors.title: Final proof only invokes the unsupported quoted theorem
errors.errored_block:
The map \(f\) is a degree-one map of pairs
\[

\longrightarrow (S,\partial S)

with \(\Dil_2(f)\leq 1\). Hence Theorem~\ref{qt:guth} applies and gives
\[

=
